title: chopchop v2: a web tool for the next generation of crispr genome engineering
display_name: CHOPCHOP v2: a web tool for the next generation of CRISPR genome engineering
abstract: in just 3 years crispr genome editing has transformed biology, and its popularity and potency continue to grow. new crispr effectors and rules for locating optimum targets continue to be reported, highlighting the need for computational crispr targeting tools to compile these rules and facilitate target selection and design. chopchop is one of the most widely used web tools for crispr- and talen-based genome editing. its overarching principle is to provide an intuitive and powerful tool that can serve both novice and experienced users. in this major update we introduce tools for the next generation of crispr advances, including cpf1 and cas9 nickases. we support a number of new features that improve the targeting power, usability and efficiency of chopchop. to increase targeting range and specificity we provide support for custom length sgrnas, and we evaluate the sequence composition of the whole sgrna and its surrounding region using models compiled from multiple large-scale studies. these and other new features, coupled with an updated interface for increased usability and support for a continually growing list of organisms, maintain chopchop as one of the leading tools for crispr genome editing. chopchop v2 can be found at http://chopchop.cbu.uib.no.
classification_path: Natural Science > Biological Science > Genetics > Genetic Engineering

title: the impact of framing on acceptance of cultured meat
display_name: The Impact of Framing on Acceptance of Cultured Meat
abstract: cultured meat can be produced from growing animal cells in-vitro rather than as part of a living animal. this technology has the potential to address several of the major ethical, environmental, and public health concerns associated with conventional meat production. however, research has highlighted some consumer uncertainty regarding the concept. although several studies have examined the media coverage of this new food technology, research linking different frames to differences in consumer attitudes is lacking. in an experimental study, we expose u.s. adults ( n = 480) to one of three different frames on cultured meat: "societal benefits," "high tech," and "same meat." we demonstrate that those who encounter cultured meat through the "high tech" frame have significantly more negative attitudes toward the concept, and are significantly less likely to consume it. worryingly, this has been a very dominant frame in early media coverage of cultured meat. whilst this is arguably inevitable, since its technologically advanced nature is what makes it newsworthy, we argue that this high tech framing may be causing consumers to develop more negative attitudes toward cultured meat than they otherwise might. implications for producers and researchers are discussed.
classification_path: Natural Science > Biological Science > Genetics > Genetic Engineering

title: heterozygosity-fitness correlations: a time for reappraisal
display_name: HETEROZYGOSITY-FITNESS CORRELATIONS: A TIME FOR REAPPRAISAL

authorships.name: Nicolas Bierne
institutions: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

authorships.name: Patrice David
institutions: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

abstract: owing to the remarkable progress of molecular techniques, heterozygosity-fitness correlations (hfcs) have become a popular tool to study the impact of inbreeding in natural populations. however, their underlying mechanisms are often hotly debated. here we argue that these "debates" rely on verbal arguments with no basis in existing theory and inappropriate statistical testing, and that it is time to reconcile hfc with its historical and theoretical fundaments. we show that available data are quantitatively and qualitatively consistent with inbreeding-based theory. hfc can be used to estimate the impact of inbreeding in populations, although such estimates are bound to be imprecise, especially when inbreeding is weak. contrary to common belief, linkage disequilibrium is not an alternative to inbreeding, but rather comes with some forms of inbreeding, and is not restricted to closely linked loci. finally, the contribution of local chromosomal effects to hfc, while predicted by inbreeding theory, is expected to be small, and has rarely if ever proven statistically significant using adequate tests. we provide guidelines to safely interpret and quantify hfcs, and present how hfcs can be used to quantify inbreeding load and unravel the structure of natural populations.
classification_path: Natural Science > Biological Science > Genetics > Genetic Engineering

title: interactive effects of drought and pathogens in forest trees
display_name: Interactive effects of drought and pathogens in forest trees

authorships.name: Louis-Michel Nageleisen
institutions: Ministère de l'Agriculture et de la Souveraineté alimentaire

abstract: this review synthesizes the available knowledge on drought-disease interactions in forest trees with a focus on (1) evidence and patterns of drought-disease interactions, (2) current understanding of processes and mechanisms, and (3) three well documented cases studies. the first part is based on the analysis of a database of slightly more than one hundred studies, obtained by keyword searches combining drought, diseases or pathogens, and forest trees. a large majority of published studies referred to a positive association between drought and disease, i.e. disease favoured by drought or drought and disease acting synergistically on tree health status, with a predominance of canker/dieback diseases, caused by pathogens like botryosphaeria, sphaeropsis, cytospora and biscognauxia (hypoxylon). the type of disease-related variables (incidence vs. severity) and the intensity and timing of water stress were shown to be significant factors affecting the drought- infection interaction. interactions with other abiotic stresses and species-specific and genetic effects, related to host or pathogen, have also been reported. direct effects of drought on pathogens are generally negative, although most fungal pathogens exhibit an important plasticity and can grow at water potentials well below the minimum for growth of their host plants. studies on indirect effects of drought on pathogens through other community interactions are still relatively scarce. positive drought-infection effects can mostly be explained by indirect effects of drought on host physiology. the predisposition and the multiple stress hypotheses are presented, as well as recent developments in the study of the molecular basis of abiotic and biotic stress, and their interactions. sphaeropsis sapinea on pines, biscognauxia mediterranea on oaks and root pathogens in declines associated with drought provide illustrative examples, treated as case studies, of pathogens of current significance associated with drought. the conclusion highlights some knowledge gaps, e.g. the role of latent parasites and the shift to a pathogenic stage, or the genetics of some fungal groups. the need for prevention of pathogen dispersal, especially crucial in the case of latent pathogens, is emphasized.

title: early aging and age-related pathologies in mice deficient in bmal1, the core componentof the circadian clock
display_name: Early aging and age-related pathologies in mice deficient in BMAL1, the core componentof the circadian clock
abstract: mice deficient in the circadian transcription factor bmal1 (brain and muscle arnt-like protein) have impaired circadian behavior and demonstrate loss of rhythmicity in the expression of target genes. here we report that bmal1 / mice have reduced lifespans and display various symptoms of premature aging including sarcopenia, cataracts, less subcutaneous fat, organ shrinkage, and others. the early aging phenotype correlates with increased levels of reactive oxygen species in some tissues of the bmal1 / animals. these findings, together with data on clock/bmal1-dependent control of stress responses, may provide a mechanistic explanation for the early onset of age-related pathologies in the absence of bmal1.
classification_path: Natural Science > Biological Science > Genetics > Genetic Engineering

title: role of a single aquaporin isoform in root water uptake
display_name: Role of a Single Aquaporin Isoform in Root Water Uptake

authorships.name: Hélène Javot
institutions: Institut des Sciences des Plantes de Montpellier

authorships.name: Virginie Lauvergeat
institutions: Institut des Sciences des Plantes de Montpellier

authorships.name: Véronique Santoni
institutions: Institut des Sciences des Plantes de Montpellier

authorships.name: J.A. Heyes
institutions: Institut des Sciences des Plantes de Montpellier

authorships.name: David Bouchez
institutions: Département Santé des Plantes et Environnement

authorships.name: Christophe Maurel
institutions: Institut des Sciences des Plantes de Montpellier

abstract: aquaporins are ubiquitous channel proteins that facilitate the transport of water across cell membranes. aquaporins show a typically high isoform multiplicity in plants, with 35 homologs in arabidopsis. the integrated function of plant aquaporins and the function of each individual isoform remain poorly understood. matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight analyses suggested that plasma membrane intrinsic protein2;2 (pip2;2) is one of the abundantly expressed aquaporin isoforms in arabidopsis root plasma membranes. two independent arabidopsis knockout mutants of pip2;2 were isolated using a pcr-based strategy from a library of plant lines mutagenized by the insertion of agrobacterium tumefaciens t-dna. expression in transgenic arabidopsis of a pip2;2 promoter-beta-glucuronidase gene fusion indicated that pip2;2 is expressed predominantly in roots, with a strong expression in the cortex, endodermis, and stele. the hydraulic conductivity of root cortex cells, as measured with a cell pressure probe, was reduced by 25 to 30% in the two allelic pip2;2 mutants compared with the wild type. in addition, free exudation measurements revealed a 14% decrease, with respect to wild-type values, in the osmotic hydraulic conductivity of roots excised from the two pip2;2 mutants. together, our data provide evidence for the contribution of a single aquaporin gene to root water uptake and identify pip2;2 as an aquaporin specialized in osmotic fluid transport. pip2;2 has a close homolog, pip2;3, showing 96.8% amino acid identity. the phenotype of pip2;2 mutants demonstrates that, despite their high homology and isoform multiplicity, plant aquaporins have evolved with nonredundant functions.
classification_path: Natural Science > Biological Science > Genetics > Genetic Engineering

title: agricultural biotechnology: the promise and prospects of genetically modified crops
display_name: Agricultural Biotechnology: The Promise and Prospects of Genetically Modified Crops
abstract: for millennia, humans have modified plant genes in order to develop crops best suited for food, fiber, feed, and energy production. conventional plant breeding remains inherently random and slow, constrained by the availability of desirable traits in closely related plant species. in contrast, agricultural biotechnology employs the modern tools of genetic engineering to reduce uncertainty and breeding time and to transfer traits from more distantly related plants. critics express concerns that the technology imposes negative environmental effects and jeopardizes the health of those who consume the frankenfoods. supporters emphasize potential gains from boosting output and lowering food prices for consumers. they argue that such gains are achieved contemporaneous with the adoption of farming practices that lower agrochemical use and lessen soil. the extensive experience with agricultural biotechnology since 1996 provides ample evidence with which to test the claims of supporters and opponents and to evaluate the prospects of genetic crop engineering. in this paper, we begin with an overview of the adoption of the first generation of agricultural biotechnology crops. we then look at the evidence on the effects of these crops: on output and prices, on the environment, and on consumer health. finally, we consider intellectual property issues surrounding this new technology.
classification_path: Natural Science > Biological Science > Genetics > Genetic Engineering

title: voluntary food labeling: the additive effect of free from labels and region of origin
display_name: Voluntary food labeling: The additive effect of “free from” labels and region of origin
abstract: abstract this study analyzes the effect of voluntary food labeling, with focus on genetically modified organisms (gmo), pesticide usage, and region of origin. we focus on medjool dates because though u.s. production of this crop has rapidly grown in recent years, no research exists related to consumers preferences and wtp for this crop. we conducted online choice experiments with a sample of over 1,400 consumers from the u.s. to determine wtp for production and region of origin labeling accounting for simultaneous versus individual labeling. results indicate consumers prefer dates grown in arizona over dates not labeled for region of origin. also, pesticide free and gmo free dates are preferred, with pesticide free having a larger impact on choices. furthermore, accounting for interactions between these two labels reveals that they can be considered subadditive in that labeling the product with both designations reduces wtp relative to pesticide free labeling only. [econlit citations: m31, q13]
classification_path: Natural Science > Biological Science > Genetics > Genetic Engineering

title: human-competitive results produced by genetic programming
display_name: Human-competitive results produced by genetic programming
abstract: genetic programming has now been used to produce at least 76 instances of results that are competitive with human-produced results. these human-competitive results come from a wide variety of fields, including quantum computing circuits, analog electrical circuits, antennas, mechanical systems, controllers, game playing, finite algebras, photonic systems, image recognition, optical lens systems, mathematical algorithms, cellular automata rules, bioinformatics, sorting networks, robotics, assembly code generation, software repair, scheduling, communication protocols, symbolic regression, reverse engineering, and empirical model discovery. this paper observes that, despite considerable variation in the techniques employed by the various researchers and research groups that produced these human-competitive results, many of the results share several common features. many of the results were achieved by using a developmental process and by using native representations regularly used by engineers in the fields involved. the best individual in the initial generation of the run of genetic programming often contains only a small number of operative parts. most of the results that duplicated the functionality of previously issued patents were novel solutions, not infringing solutions. in addition, the production of human-competitive results, as well as the increased intricacy of the results, are broadly correlated to increased availability of computing power tracked by moore's law. the paper ends by predicting that the increased availability of computing power (through both parallel computing and moore's law) should result in the production, in the future, of an increasing flow of human-competitive results, as well as more intricate and impressive results.
classification_path: Natural Science > Biological Science > Genetics > Genetic Engineering

title: exploring the decision making process of canadian organic food consumers
display_name: Exploring the decision‐making process of Canadian organic food consumers
abstract: abstract purpose although consumption of organic food (of) shows promising trends in canada, there is no clear understanding of the barriers that still prevent a larger demand for of. the main objectives of this paper are to understand what, how, where, and why canadian consumers buy of by exploring consumers' motivations and decision making process, and digging into consumers' trust orientations with regards to of. design/methodology/approach in depth interviews are conducted and data collected are analyzed using content analysis. findings results indicate that canadian typical organic product consumers have a defined purchase scheme in terms of retail stores selection and price, as well as values and trust orientations. they identify health, the environment, and support for local farmers as their primary motivators for organic consumption. in particular, health motivation is mainly based on avoidance from chemical residues, antibiotics, hormones, genetically modified organisms, and diseases. results also show that distribution, certification, country of origin, and labeling are all related to consumers' level of trust when consuming of. research limitations/implications data collection was conducted in only one canadian city and should be extended to other cities across the country. originality/value this paper entails an exploration of consumer's decision making process and their underlying motivations and trust orientations but also an investigation of the marketing mix related to of.
classification_path: Natural Science > Biological Science > Genetics > Genetic Engineering

title: the evolution of the plastid chromosome in land plants: gene content, gene order, gene function
display_name: The evolution of the plastid chromosome in land plants: gene content, gene order, gene function
abstract: this review bridges functional and evolutionary aspects of plastid chromosome architecture in land plants and their putative ancestors. we provide an overview on the structure and composition of the plastid genome of land plants as well as the functions of its genes in an explicit phylogenetic and evolutionary context. we will discuss the architecture of land plant plastid chromosomes, including gene content and synteny across land plants. moreover, we will explore the functions and roles of plastid encoded genes in metabolism and their evolutionary importance regarding gene retention and conservation. we suggest that the slow mode at which the plastome typically evolves is likely to be influenced by a combination of different molecular mechanisms. these include the organization of plastid genes in operons, the usually uniparental mode of plastid inheritance, the activity of highly effective repair mechanisms as well as the rarity of plastid fusion. nevertheless, structurally rearranged plastomes can be found in several unrelated lineages (e.g. ferns, pinaceae, multiple angiosperm families). rearrangements and gene losses seem to correlate with an unusual mode of plastid transmission, abundance of repeats, or a heterotrophic lifestyle (parasites or myco-heterotrophs). while only a few functional gene gains and more frequent gene losses have been inferred for land plants, the plastid ndh complex is one example of multiple independent gene losses and will be discussed in detail. patterns of ndh-gene loss and functional analyses indicate that these losses are usually found in plant groups with a certain degree of heterotrophy, might rendering plastid encoded ndh1 subunits dispensable.
classification_path: Natural Science > Biological Science > Genetics > Genetic Engineering

title: high lipid induction in microalgae for biodiesel production
display_name: High Lipid Induction in Microalgae for Biodiesel Production
abstract: oil-accumulating microalgae have the potential to enable large-scale biodiesel production without competing for arable land or biodiverse natural landscapes. high lipid productivity of dominant, fast-growing algae is a major prerequisite for commercial production of microalgal oil-derived biodiesel. however, under optimal growth conditions, large amounts of algal biomass are produced, but with relatively low lipid contents, while species with high lipid contents are typically slow growing. major advances in this area can be made through the induction of lipid biosynthesis, e.g., by environmental stresses. lipids, in the form of triacylglycerides typically provide a storage function in the cell that enables microalgae to endure adverse environmental conditions. essentially algal biomass and triacylglycerides compete for photosynthetic assimilate and a reprogramming of physiological pathways is required to stimulate lipid biosynthesis. there has been a wide range of studies carried out to identify and develop efficient lipid induction techniques in microalgae such as nutrients stress (e.g., nitrogen and/or phosphorus starvation), osmotic stress, radiation, ph, temperature, heavy metals and other chemicals. in addition, several genetic strategies for increased triacylglycerides production and inducibility are currently being developed. in this review, we discuss the potential of lipid induction techniques in microalgae and also their application at commercial scale for the production of biodiesel.
classification_path: Natural Science > Biological Science > Genetics > Genetic Engineering

title: integrated multi-omics of the human gut microbiome in a case study of familial type 1 diabetes
display_name: Integrated multi-omics of the human gut microbiome in a case study of familial type 1 diabetes
abstract: abstract the gastrointestinal microbiome is a complex ecosystem with functions that shape human health. studying the relationship between taxonomic alterations and functional repercussions linked to disease remains challenging. here, we present an integrative approach to resolve the taxonomic and functional attributes of gastrointestinal microbiota at the metagenomic, metatranscriptomic and metaproteomic levels. we apply our methods to samples from four families with multiple cases of type 1 diabetes mellitus (t1dm). analysis of intra- and inter-individual variation demonstrates that family membership has a pronounced effect on the structural and functional composition of the gastrointestinal microbiome. in the context of t1dm, consistent taxonomic differences were absent across families, but certain human exocrine pancreatic proteins were found at lower levels. the associated microbial functional signatures were linked to metabolic traits in distinct taxa. the methodologies and results provide a foundation for future large-scale integrated multi-omic analyses of the gastrointestinal microbiome in the context of host microbe interactions in human health and disease.
classification_path: Natural Science > Biological Science > Genetics > Genetic Engineering

title: gnotobiotic mouse model of phage bacterial host dynamics in the human gut
display_name: Gnotobiotic mouse model of phage–bacterial host dynamics in the human gut
abstract: significance a consortium of sequenced human gut bacteria was introduced into germ-free mice followed by a staged phage attack with virus-like particles purified from the fecal microbiota of five healthy adult humans. unique phages were identified attacking microbiota members in nonsimultaneous fashion. some host bacterial species acquired resistance to phage attack through ecological or epigenetic mechanisms. changes in community structure observed after attack were transient. spontaneous induction of prophages present in seven bacterial taxa was modest, occurring independently of the phage attack. together, these results reveal a largely temperate phage bacterial host dynamic and illustrate how gnotobiotic mouse models can help characterize ecological relationships in the gut by taking into account its most abundant but least understood component, viruses.
classification_path: Natural Science > Biological Science > Genetics > Genetic Engineering

title: genetic improvement for aquaculture species: a promising approach for aquaculture challenges and development
display_name: Genetic improvement for aquaculture species: A promising approach for aquaculture challenges and development
abstract: with the fast-growing population and rising prosperity in the world, producing a sufficient amount of animal-based food products has become a critical challenge faced by mankind. nowadays, arable land has almost been fully utilized, and capture fisheries cannot provide sufficient yield (fao 2020). however, aquaculture is, globally, the fastest growing farmed food production sector, showing 5.3% increase annually from 2001 to 2018 (fao 2020). however, there are still some severe bottlenecks in the development of aquaculture. firstly, the majority of aquaculture production is from a small number of culture species. over 90% of finfish production involves just 27 species/species groups (see the details in ref. 2). as compared with hundreds- or thousands-of-years domestication of crops, most aquaculture species have a short or even a recent history of domestication, and some of which are even just newly introduced into aquaculture.2, 3 secondly, insufficient growth, sexual precocity, wide occurrence of diseases, reduced products quality, impaired animal welfare and environmental pollution issues, which are commonly seen in most of the farmed aquatic animals, are also significantly hindering the sustainable development of aquaculture. either in crops or livestock, genetic improvement technologies have been incorporated to promote food production, disease prevention, product quality and environmental protection.4, 5 so far, cross-breeding, mutation breeding, transgenic breeding and breeding by genome editing are the four main genetic improvement technologies applied in crops culture,4 and the individual or comprehensive application of these technologies have shown irreplaceable benefits in solving practical problems. accordingly, these genetic improvement technologies have also been applied in aquaculture research and practice. although the history of genetic improvement technologies in aquaculture is relatively shorter than that of crops and livestock, some genetically improved aquaculture species, for example, donaldson strain rainbow trout oncorhynchus mykiss, norwegian atlantic salmon salmo salar and genetically improved farmed tilapia (gift) oreochromis niloticus, have shown considerably higher economic benefits than their unselected relatives. in addition, the application of genetic improvement technologies in aquaculture also significantly helps to increase disease resistance, deposition of omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids and environmental friendship. however, the huge diversity of aquaculture species, relatively short culture histories of most species and different administrative focuses amongst countries, also bring big challenges in the application of genetic improvement technologies in aquaculture. in this issue, two review articles and one opinion article are published in this respect. in the review article focussing on the uk aquaculture, regan et al5 summarized the success via selective breeding in obtaining atlantic salmon with some important economic traits, including fast growth, delayed sexual maturity, and disease resistance against infectious pancreatic necrosis virus (ipnv). it was also introduced in this review paper that a series of economically important traits, such as growth, year-round growth, survival, fillet colour, sexual maturation, nutritional requirement, feed conversion efficiency, environmental sensitivity and disease resistance have been the cores of research and developmental programmes in the united kingdom. in addition, this review paper highlighted that the gene deletion strategy using crispr may provide an efficient and valuable tool in understanding the possible functions or mechanisms of genes and their variations in controlling these traits. therefore, the authors concluded that the increased adoption of modern breeding technologies will assist the uk aquaculture industries to remain competitive in a global market. on the other hand, in a global market, it is crucial that these modern tools and technologies are embraced and developed to maintain the sustainable development of the farming of salmons and other aquaculture species in the future. in another review article,3 the authors retrieved the latest research on genome editing of aquaculture finfish species. particularly, this article introduced the targeted alterations of fish genomes and the site-specific nucleases (ssn). accordingly, four categories of site-directed nucleases, including meganucleases, zfn, talen and crispr were reviewed in detail. in this review, some technical challenges are also analysed when using crispr technology in finfish, including off-target mutations, effect of whole-genome duplications and mosaicism. in the latter part of this article, authors introduced also some regulative frameworks for conducting genome editing on finfish in different countries, which could affect how a country can, and has to, maintain genome modified and/or edited organisms towards safeguarding environmental sustainability and biodiversity. the main points in the above two review articles are supported by an opinion article published as well in the present issue.2 the authors of this opinion article analysed the possible factors limiting the development and adoption of genetically improved fish stocks, including long-term commitment of financial support, technical training and development of effective business models for benefit-sharing amongst breeders, seed producers and farmers. the authors also introduced several successful models for the development and distribution of genetically improved aquaculture species, such as private- or public sectors and their collaborations. based on these models and the related analysis, some important regional opportunities were identified in order to contribute to regional economic development, food security and human well-being, especially in low-income economies. nevertheless, in the end, the authors appealed to consider the sustainability of harvests from the wild and of genetic resource usage for future selective breeding. considering the importance of genetic improvement in developing aquaculture, these three aligned articles are published in this issue, which together comprehensively present the current knowledge and scientific viewpoints in the field. the use of genetic improvement techniques in aquaculture will promisingly enable the understanding of important traits and the creation of enhanced, high performing, efficient and sustainable aquaculture species in the future.

title: complete mitochondrial genome phylogeographic analysis of killer whales ( orcinus orca ) indicates multiple species
display_name: Complete mitochondrial genome phylogeographic analysis of killer whales (Orcinus orca) indicates multiple species

authorships.name: Phillip A. Morin
institutions: NOAA National Marine Fisheries Service Southwest Fisheries Science Center

authorships.name: Frederick I. Archer
institutions: NOAA National Marine Fisheries Service Southwest Fisheries Science Center

authorships.name: Paul R. Wade
institutions: NOAA National Marine Fisheries Service Alaska Fisheries Science Center

authorships.name: John Durban
institutions: NOAA National Marine Fisheries Service Alaska Fisheries Science Center

authorships.name: Kim M. Parsons
institutions: NOAA National Marine Fisheries Service Alaska Fisheries Science Center

authorships.name: Robert L. Pitman
institutions: NOAA National Marine Fisheries Service Southwest Fisheries Science Center

abstract: killer whales ( orcinus orca ) currently comprise a single, cosmopolitan species with a diverse diet. however, studies over the last 30 yr have revealed populations of sympatric ecotypes with discrete prey preferences, morphology, and behaviors. although these ecotypes avoid social interactions and are not known to interbreed, genetic studies to date have found extremely low levels of diversity in the mitochondrial control region, and few clear phylogeographic patterns worldwide. this low level of diversity is likely due to low mitochondrial mutation rates that are common to cetaceans. using killer whales as a case study, we have developed a method to readily sequence, assemble, and analyze complete mitochondrial genomes from large numbers of samples to more accurately assess phylogeography and estimate divergence times. this represents an important tool for wildlife management, not only for killer whales but for many marine taxa. we used high-throughput sequencing to survey whole mitochondrial genome variation of 139 samples from the north pacific, north atlantic, and southern oceans. phylogenetic analysis indicated that each of the known ecotypes represents a strongly supported clade with divergence times ranging from 150,000 to 700,000 yr ago. we recommend that three named ecotypes be elevated to full species, and that the remaining types be recognized as subspecies pending additional data. establishing appropriate taxonomic designations will greatly aid in understanding the ecological impacts and conservation needs of these important marine predators. we predict that phylogeographic mitogenomics will become an important tool for improved statistical phylogeography and more precise estimates of divergence times.
classification_path: Natural Science > Biological Science > Genetics > Genetic Engineering

title: long-term forest soil warming alters microbial communities in temperate forest soils
display_name: Long-term forest soil warming alters microbial communities in temperate forest soils
abstract: soil microbes are major drivers of soil carbon cycling, yet we lack an understanding of how climate warming will affect microbial communities. three ongoing field studies at the harvard forest long-term ecological research (lter) site (petersham, ma) have warmed soils 5 c above ambient temperatures for 5, 8, and 20 years. we used this chronosequence to test the hypothesis that soil microbial communities have changed in response to chronic warming. bacterial community composition was studied using illumina sequencing of the 16s ribosomal rna gene, and bacterial and fungal abundance were assessed using quantitative pcr. only the 20-year warmed site exhibited significant change in bacterial community structure in the organic soil horizon, with no significant changes in the mineral soil. the dominant taxa, abundant at 0.1% or greater, represented 0.3% of the richness but nearly 50% of the observations (sequences). individual members of the actinobacteria, alphaproteobacteria and acidobacteria showed strong warming responses, with one actinomycete decreasing from 4.5 to 1% relative abundance with warming. ribosomal rna copy number can obfuscate community profiles, but is also correlated with maximum growth rate or trophic strategy among bacteria. ribosomal rna copy number correction did not affect community profiles, but rrna copy number was significantly decreased in warming plots compared to controls. increased bacterial evenness, shifting beta diversity, decreased fungal abundance and increased abundance of bacteria with low rrna operon copy number, including alphaproteobacteria and acidobacteria, together suggest that more or alternative niche space is being created over the course of long-term warming.
classification_path: Natural Science > Biological Science > Genetics > Genetic Engineering

title: subversion of cellular autophagosomal machinery by rna viruses
display_name: Subversion of Cellular Autophagosomal Machinery by RNA Viruses
abstract: infection of human cells with poliovirus induces the proliferation of double-membraned cytoplasmic vesicles whose surfaces are used as the sites of viral rna replication and whose origin is unknown. here, we show that several hallmarks of cellular autophagosomes can be identified in poliovirus-induced vesicles, including colocalization of lamp1 and lc3, the human homolog of saccharomyces cerevisiae atg8p, and staining with the fluorophore monodansylcadaverine followed by fixation. colocalization of lc3 and lamp1 was observed early in the poliovirus replicative cycle, in cells infected with rhinoviruses 2 and 14, and in cells that express poliovirus proteins 2bc and 3a, known to be sufficient to induce double-membraned vesicles. stimulation of autophagy increased poliovirus yield, and inhibition of the autophagosomal pathway by 3-methyladenine or by rna interference against mrnas that encode two different proteins known to be required for autophagy decreased poliovirus yield. we propose that, for poliovirus and rhinovirus, components of the cellular machinery of autophagosome formation are subverted to promote viral replication. although autophagy can serve in the innate immune response to microorganisms, our findings are inconsistent with a role for the induced autophagosome-like structures in clearance of poliovirus. instead, we argue that these double-membraned structures provide membranous supports for viral rna replication complexes, possibly enabling the nonlytic release of cytoplasmic contents, including progeny virions, from infected cells.

title: nrf2, a guardian of healthspan and gatekeeper of species longevity
display_name: Nrf2, a Guardian of Healthspan and Gatekeeper of Species Longevity

authorships.name: Kaitlyn N. Lewis
institutions: The University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio

authorships.name: James Mele
institutions: The University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio

authorships.name: John D. Hayes
institutions: The University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio

authorships.name: Rochelle Buffenstein
institutions: The University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio

abstract: although aging is a ubiquitous process that prevails in all organisms, the mechanisms governing both the rate of decline in functionality and the age of onset remain elusive. a profound constitutively upregulated cytoprotective response is commonly observed in naturally long-lived species and experimental models of extensions to lifespan (e.g., genetically-altered and/or experimentally manipulated organisms), as indicated by enhanced resistance to stress and upregulated downstream components of the cytoprotective nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (nrf2)-signaling pathway. the transcription factor nrf2 is constitutively expressed in all tissues, although levels may vary among organs, with the key detoxification organs (kidney and liver) exhibiting highest levels. nrf2 may be further induced by cellular stressors including endogenous reactive-oxygen species or exogenous electrophiles. the nrf2-signaling pathway mediates multiple avenues of cytoprotection by activating the transcription of more than 200 genes that are crucial in the metabolism of drugs and toxins, protection against oxidative stress and inflammation, as well as playing an integral role in stability of proteins and in the removal of damaged proteins via proteasomal degradation or autophagy. nrf2 interacts with other important cell regulators such as tumor suppressor protein 53 (p53) and nuclear factor-kappa beta (nf- b) and through their combined interactions is the guardian of healthspan, protecting against many age-related diseases including cancer and neurodegeneration. we hypothesize that this signaling pathway plays a critical role in the determination of species longevity and that this pathway may indeed be the master regulator of the aging process.

title: the ongoing debate on nbts and possible roads for the future
display_name: The ongoing debate on NBTs and possible roads for the future
abstract: there are marked differences in the approaches that regulate genetically modified (gm) products and the new breeding techniques (nbts) in the european union (eu) and in other areas of the world. through the review of regulations and ongoing discussions, we show that the world can be divided in two groups based on the discrepancies in the approach of the country's regulations. on the one hand, europe, with the main countries of asia and africa, regulates new breeding techniques as a genetically modified organism. on the other, a group of countries mainly located in the american continent, together with australia, adopted a case-by-case approach, and are generally at a more advanced stage in the implementation of these new techniques. the paper aims to evaluate the possible evolution in the countries' regulations on the use of nbts in the next years. the division between western and eastern countries of the world is confirmed, with some interesting movements in some regions. greater uniformity among national regulations would be desirable to promote the implementation of biotechnologies in agriculture. the main research findings are that most eu member states have taken a conservative position, whereas the eastern group is more advanced and this could be a driving force for some regions toward acceptance of these technologies in the coming years.

title: general hypotheses in invasion ecology
display_name: General hypotheses in invasion ecology
abstract: every scientific discipline needs concepts and hypotheses these are the backbones of science. their development over time also reflects the growth or decline, respectively, of scientific disciplines. here, i focus on general hypotheses in invasion ecology, a rapidly growing discipline (richardson & ricciardi, 2013). the publication of the book the ecology of invasions by animals and plants by charles elton (1958) is usually seen as the start of modern invasion ecology. stressing modern is important here, as earlier researchers also investigated this topic, for example darwin (1859; cadotte, 2006). kowarik & py ek (2012) offer insights into the history of invasion ecology with a focus on the swiss botanist albert thellung (1881 1928) who took the first steps towards unifying concepts and hypotheses in invasion ecology. fifty years after the publication of elton's book, a special issue of diversity and distributions was dedicated to elton's legacy. an editorial in this special issue outlined how influential elton and his work remains today (richardson & py ek, 2008). elton's 1958 book is the most frequently cited source in the field, and several of invasion ecology's current major hypotheses can be found there, for example the biotic resistance hypothesis (richardson & py ek, 2007). in the following, i will focus on this hypothesis and three other influential invasion hypotheses, and studies that have tested them. these hypotheses were arbitrarily selected (see catford et al., 2009; lamarque et al., 2011; jeschke et al., 2012a,b; lockwood et al., 2013; lowry et al., 2013; and references therein for other influential invasion hypotheses). i give a definition (but be aware that different framings exist for each hypothesis; heger et al., 2013) and summarize two selected articles published in diversity and distributions on each hypothesis (these articles appear in bold). the hypotheses are ordered chronologically, from oldest to youngest. i will also outline an approach to synthesize invasion hypotheses, and end with the question where to from here? the biotic resistance hypothesis, which i use synonymously with the diversity-invasibility hypothesis here, posits that ecosystems with high biodiversity are more resistant to invaders than ecosystems with low biodiversity (elton, 1958; levine & d'antonio, 1999; lonsdale, 1999; jeschke et al., 2012a,b). it is a classic hypothesis of the field that is, like most other invasion hypotheses, strongly connected with general ecological hypotheses and concepts (box 1). the resistance hypothesis has been empirically tested in multiple ways. the most common test is to compare native species richness with alien species richness, where the latter is used as an inverse measure of biotic resistance: high alien species richness indicates low resistance. although this approach does not control for the number of introduced species, it was used by 57 of 129 tests (44%) of the hypothesis identified by jeschke et al. (2012a). the resistance hypothesis predicts that native and alien species richness are negatively correlated, but a number of studies published at the turn of the century and thereafter reported the opposite pattern. a positive correlation was, for example, reported by mckinney (2002) for alien plants in 77 protected areas in the usa. findings like these have led to the formulation of the rich-get-richer pattern and the acceptance hypothesis, positing that the relationship between native and alien species richness is typically positive, particularly at large spatial scales (stohlgren et al., 2003, 2006). in some cases, complex patterns can be found. for example, espinosa-garc a et al. (2004) reported for plants in mexico a negative relationship between alien and native weed species richness (in line with the resistance hypothesis and contrary to the acceptance hypothesis); on the other hand, they reported a positive relationship between alien weed species richness and native non-weed species richness (in line with the acceptance hypothesis and contrary to the resistance hypothesis). in general, most tests of the resistance hypothesis focused on terrestrial plants and reported low empirical support (jeschke et al., 2012a,b). the latter is particularly true for large spatial scales, as studies conducted at small scales have more frequently reported supporting evidence (fridley et al., 2007). it is sometimes argued that invasion ecology is isola-ted from the rest of ecology (e.g. davis et al., 2001). although stronger connections between researchers working on biological invasions and those focusing on other ecological topics would certainly be beneficial, a look at the concepts and hypotheses in invasion ecology reveals that these are deeply connected with those in general ecology. let us look at the biotic resistance hypothesis (see also main text) as an example. this hypothesis is a special formulation of a more general ecological hypothesis, namely the diversity-stability hypothesis which states that ecosystems with high biodiversity are more stable than ecosystems with low biodiversity (ives & carpenter, 2007; jeschke et al., 2012a, 2013). in the biotic resistance hypothesis (treated synonymously here with the diversity-invasibility hypothesis), stability is replaced by resistance against invaders. the resistance hypothesis is also related to the concept of the ecological niche, one of ecology's most fundamental ideas. the ecological niche has been defined differently by different authors, as outlined by pulliam (2000), p. 351: hutchinson (1957) used the word niche to refer to the environmental requirements of a species, whereas earlier authors, especially elton (1927) and grinnell (1917), had used the term niche to refer to a place or recess in the environment that has the potential to support a species according to hutchinson, species, not environments, have niches. and for elton, environments have niches. these can be vacant, and the probability that a niche is vacant is higher if there are fewer species, genera, life-forms etc. in an ecosystem as compared to an ecosystem with many species, genera, life-forms etc. where most niches are filled. consequently, ecosystems with high biodiversity should offer fewer niche opportunities for invaders (i.e. they should be more resistant against invaders) than ecosystems with low biodiversity. this brief treatment of the biotic resistance hypothesis shows its strong connection to general ecology. as a consequence, studies testing this and many other invasion hypotheses can reveal insights that are not only relevant for invasion ecology but for ecology in general and other disciplines as well (sax et al., 2005, 2007). taking this perspective, invasion ecology is not isolated at all but well connected with other (sub)disciplines. another influential invasion hypothesis is the tens rule which posits that approximately 10% of species successfully take consecutive steps of the invasion process: about 10% of species transported beyond their native range will be released or escape in the wild (they are called introduced species or casuals); about 10% of these introduced species will be able to establish themselves in the wild (they are called naturalized species); and about 10% of species established will become invasive/pest species (williamson & brown, 1986; williamson, 1996; jeschke et al., 2012a,b). this rule from the late 1980s became popular in the 1990s which is when total numbers of publications on biological invasions started to rise (richardson & py ek, 2008). the tens rule is of high practical importance, for example for cost-benefit models (keller et al., 2007) and has also been applied to genetically modified organisms (regal, 1993; williamson, 1993). caley et al. (2008) outlined a bayesian approach for estimating the proportion of introduced species that will establish themselves. their approach considers the important issue that if simply taking the ratio of established to introduced species for testing the tens rule, one is assuming that all introduced species have had enough time to actually establish themselves. this may not be the case (see also kowarik, 1995; jeschke & strayer, 2005). they applied their approach to data from woody plants introduced to south australia and estimated the probability of naturalization to be 18.6%, with the 95% confidence interval ranging from 15.5 to 23.4%. while the confidence interval does not overlap with the 10% predicted by the tens rule, the 18.6% estimate is inside the 5 20% interval that was suggested by williamson (1996) for comparison of the tens rule with empirical data (see also jeschke et al., 2012a). k iv nek & py ek (2006) also looked at woody species, but in this case those introduced to the czech republic. of 180 species commonly planted there for at least 60 years and well adapted to the conditions of the target region, 57 (31.7%) have taken the first step of the invasion process (i.e. they have become casuals at least), 28 (49.1% of 57 species) have naturalized and 17 (60.7% of 28 species) have become invasive. in their discussion section, k iv nek & py ek (2006) also gave figures for the larger pool of woody plants introduced to the czech republic (not restricted to species commonly planted there for at least 60 years and well adapted to the conditions of the target region). in this larger sample, out of 127 species that have taken the first step of the invasion process, 54 (42.5%) have naturalized and 11 (20.4% of 54 species) have become pests. these figures are higher than the 10% predicted by the tens rule and are outside the 5 20% range. most studies in the field of invasion ecology have focused on plants, but most studies on the tens rule have actually focused on animals, particularly vertebrates (jeschke et al., 2012a,b). the underlying reason is most likely that reliable data for testing the rule are mainly available for vertebrates, particularly birds and mammals. yet, empirical support for the rule is particularly low for vertebrates which often show much higher transition rates than predicted by the tens rule: they are typically around 50% rather than 10%, although the data are highly variable (jeschke & strayer, 2005; jeschke, 2008). empirical support for the rule is significantly higher for plants and invertebrates than for vertebrates, but even for plants and invertebrates studies often report results that are beyond the 5 20% range (jeschke et al., 2012a). according to the enemy release hypothesis, the absence of enemies in the exotic range is a cause of invasion success (maron & vil , 2001; keane & crawley, 2002; jeschke et al., 2012a,b; heger & jeschke, 2014). although albert thellung already implicitly used the enemy release hypothesis in 1915 (kowarik & py ek, 2012), the hypothesis has only truly come alive in the last two decades. it is now very influential in the field. also, it is strongly connected with other invasion hypotheses, for instance the eica hypothesis (evolution of increased competitive ability; blossey & n tzold, 1995) or the shifting defence hypothesis (doorduin & vrieling, 2011). like other hypotheses, many different variants and specific formulations of the enemy release hypothesis have been tested. for instance, some studies looked at a potentially reduced infestation of the alien species with enemies in the exotic range, whereas other studies looked at a potentially reduced damage by enemies. an example for the latter is the study by ebeling et al. (2008) who compared 10 native chinese and 10 invasive german populations of the shrub buddleja davidii, finding reduced damage by leaf herbivores in the invasive populations. at the same time, the plants in the invasive populations were taller, had thicker stems, larger inflorescences and heavier seeds than the plants in the native populations. these results are in line with the enemy release hypothesis. ashton & lerdau (2008) did not compare native and alien populations of a given species, but compared alien with native species in the same range. they focused on vines in the us, finding no support for the prediction that alien species would suffer less damage from herbivores. what they did find, however, was that alien species are more tolerant of herbivory. these mixed results are similar to other empirical tests of the enemy release hypothesis (colautti et al., 2004; liu & stiling, 2006; hawkes, 2007; chun et al., 2010; jeschke et al., 2012a; heger & jeschke, 2014). the propagule pressure hypothesis posits that high propagule pressure is a cause of invasion success (lockwood et al., 2005). as with other invasion hypotheses, this one has been interpreted differently by different authors; in particular, the term propagule pressure has been defined and measured in various ways. typically, propagule pressure is synonymously treated with introduction effort and considered to consist of: (1) propagule size, which is the average number of individuals involved in a single release event; and (2) propagule number or frequency, which is the average number of release events per unit time (lockwood et al., 2005, 2009, 2013; blackburn et al., 2009; simberloff, 2009). the propagule pressure hypothesis has been hugely influential in 21st century invasion ecology richardson (2004), p. 317, wrote: understanding propagule pressure is the new frontier in invasion ecology. this underscores the growing realization that (a) event-level characteristics such as propagule pressure and (b) human activities (e.g. intentional or unintentional transporting and release of alien species) play a key role for biological invasions. twentieth century invasion ecology rather focused on general characteristics of invaders or invaded ecosystems (e.g. drake et al., 1989). foxcroft et al. (2004) showed that propagule pressure is highly important for understanding the invasion of south africa's kruger national park by the cactus opuntia stricta. bacon et al. (2014) combined agricultural trade databases with european quarantine interception records to estimate propagule pressure for quarantine arthropods introduced to europe. they found that propagule pressure, climate suitability and host availability of arthropods together are strongly related to their establishment patterns. overall, the propagule pressure hypothesis seems to be quite well supported by empirical evidence (lockwood et al., 2005, 2013; colautti et al., 2006; blackburn et al., 2009; simberloff, 2009; lamarque et al., 2011). although some critical tones have been raised here too (moulton et al., 2011), there seems to be more consensus on this hypothesis than on most others. the growth of invasion ecology comes with an increasing number of invasion hypotheses. several authors have offered tools and frameworks for synthesizing these hypotheses. for instance, catford et al. (2009) listed 29 invasion hypotheses and outlined a framework to connect them. key parts of this framework are propagule pressure (p), abiotic characteristics (a), biotic characteristics (b) and how humans influence p, a and b. they also note similarities among the 29 hypotheses. other tools and frameworks for synthesizing invasion hypotheses have been suggested by gurevitch et al. (2011), heger et al. (2013) and saul et al. (2013). after this review of key publications on invasion hypotheses and their synthesis, i now offer some thoughts on (1) how existing invasion hypotheses might be revised or replaced, and (2) how their synthesis can be moved forward. first, many invasion hypotheses are empirically not well supported (see above and jeschke et al., 2012a; moles et al., 2012). it thus seems that the field's progress is hampered by holding on to concepts and ideas that simply do not work, at least not under many circumstances (see also davis, 2011). as many of these ideas are intuitively appealing, invasion ecologists hesitate to revise or replace them. another reason is that in invasion ecology as in other ecological subdisciplines data are rarely crystal clear and can be criticized from many angles, for example laboratory data can be criticized for being unnatural, or observational field data can be criticized for not revealing cause effect relationships. as every research method can be criticized in one way or the other, a synthesis of studies with different methods can reveal a clearer and more robust picture. a novel approach to synthesize studies on a given major hypothesis is the hierarchy-of-hypotheses (hoh) approach suggested by jeschke et al. (2012a) and heger et al. (2013); see also heger & jeschke (2014). this approach may serve the field in revealing which hypotheses work under which circumstances, and which hypotheses should be revised or replaced. second, what i consider a promising path forward for synthesizing multiple invasion hypotheses is to apply network analysis. a network of invasion hypotheses is a powerful visualization, illustrating how the major concepts of the field are connected. a first preliminary example of such a network is shown in fig. 1. this network includes the 29 invasion hypotheses featured in catford et al. (2009) and was created based on their table 2 that gives information on similarities between the hypotheses. networks could also be constructed based on citation frequencies of key papers on each invasion hypothesis, or based on traits of invasion hypotheses. when applying the hoh approach to a network of hypotheses, each hypothesis in the network can be hierarchically divided into more specific subhypotheses. such a hierarchical network of hypotheses not only represents the combined theory of the field but can be easily connected with empirical studies on biological invasions that have tested any (sub)hypothesis. as invasion hypotheses are strongly connected with general ecological hypotheses (box 1), it will be straightforward to extend the network of hypotheses and empirical studies testing them, so that the whole field of ecology is covered. i thus believe this approach has much potential to move forward both invasion ecology and general ecology. i warmly thank david richardson for the invitation to write this editorial. i am also very grateful to martin enders for creating fig. 1, and i highly appreciate comments on the manuscript by him, tina heger and david richardson.

title: grna design: how its evolution impacted on crispr/cas9 systems refinement
display_name: gRNA Design: How Its Evolution Impacted on CRISPR/Cas9 Systems Refinement
abstract: over the past decade, genetic engineering has witnessed a revolution with the emergence of a relatively new genetic editing tool based on rna-guided nucleases: the crispr/cas9 system. since the first report in 1987 and characterization in 2007 as a bacterial defense mechanism, this system has garnered immense interest and research attention. crispr systems provide immunity to bacteria against invading genetic material; however, with specific modifications in sequence and structure, it becomes a precise editing system capable of modifying the genomes of a wide range of organisms. the refinement of these modifications encompasses diverse approaches, including the development of more accurate nucleases, understanding of the cellular context and epigenetic conditions, and the re-designing guide rnas (grnas). considering the critical importance of the correct performance of crispr/cas9 systems, our scope will emphasize the latter approach. hence, we present an overview of the past and the most recent guide rna web-based design tools, highlighting the evolution of their computational architecture and grna characteristics over the years. our study explains computational approaches that use machine learning techniques, neural networks, and grna/target interactions data to enable predictions and classifications. this review could open the door to a dynamic community that uses up-to-date algorithms to optimize and create promising grnas, suitable for modern crispr/cas9 engineering.
classification_path: Natural Science > Biological Science > Genetics > Genetic Engineering

title: economic man in cross-cultural perspective: behavioral experiments in 15 small-scale societies
display_name: “Economic man” in cross-cultural perspective: Behavioral experiments in 15 small-scale societies
abstract: researchers from across the social sciences have found consistent deviations from the predictions of the canonical model of self-interest in hundreds of experiments from around the world. this research, however, cannot determine whether the uniformity results from universal patterns of human behavior or from the limited cultural variation available among the university students used in virtually all prior experimental work. to address this, we undertook a cross-cultural study of behavior in ultimatum, public goods, and dictator games in a range of small-scale societies exhibiting a wide variety of economic and cultural conditions. we found, first, that the canonical model based on self-interest fails in all of the societies studied. second, our data reveal substantially more behavioral variability across social groups than has been found in previous research. third, group-level differences in economic organization and the structure of social interactions explain a substantial portion of the behavioral variation across societies: the higher the degree of market integration and the higher the payoffs to cooperation in everyday life, the greater the level of prosociality expressed in experimental games. fourth, the available individual-level economic and demographic variables do not consistently explain game behavior, either within or across groups. fifth, in many cases experimental play appears to reflect the common interactional patterns of everyday life.
